sources.title: Exact tagged repository question and frozen Batch 0033 source boundary
Coin-change enumeration and DP deterministic Java validation against independent triple-loop oracle

claims.text: The repository preserves N cents, 1/2/3-cent denominations, all combination ways and DP/recursion; enumerate-vs-count, supply/order semantics, language/API/range and edge conventions are answer-side contracts.
Under the explicit unlimited/order-insensitive contract, the exact fenced Java recursion enumerates each nonnegative count triple satisfying one+2*two+3*three=N exactly once.
Coin-outer amount-inner one-dimensional unbounded-knapsack DP counts those unordered combinations; exhaustive N=0..200 validation matches the independent oracle set size.

The reviewed enumeration loop uses remaining/coin for its count upper bound and DP additions use Math.addExact, avoiding an overflow-prone count*coin loop guard and failing closed on long count overflow.

findings: The exact repository source preserves N cents, denominations 1/2/3, all combination ways and an explicit DP/recursion hint; it does not preserve enumerate-versus-count semantics, supply limits, order semantics, programming language/API, N range or edge conventions.

The candidate makes unlimited supply, order-insensitive combinations, Java implementation, N=0 empty-combination and N<0 empty-result behavior explicit answer-side contracts rather than recovered source facts.

The exact displayed Java fence is byte-for-byte identical to the compiled fixture after the writer remediation; the recursion fixes denomination order and enumerates count triples rather than ordered pick sequences.
For every N from 0 through 200, enumeration is duplicate-free and exactly matches an independently implemented triple-loop oracle over nonnegative 1/2/3-cent counts.
For every N from 0 through 200, the coin-outer amount-inner unbounded-knapsack DP count equals the independent oracle set size, demonstrating combination rather than permutation semantics.

The enumeration bound uses remaining/coin rather than count*coin, avoiding an avoidable int multiplication overflow in the loop condition; DP addition uses Math.addExact to fail closed on count overflow.
The answer explains N=0, negative input, output-sensitive O(K) enumeration cost, O(N) DP cost, and the limited-supply / ordered-sequence variants without fabricating project experience.
No placeholder implementation, uncovered source variant, duplicate enumeration behavior or material unsupported claim remains in this candidate.
